rows: Legionnaires’ disease cases should be assessed for links to clusters or outbreaks.
Public-health investigation combines epidemiological and microbiological information.
Travel, healthcare and community exposures require setting-specific consideration.
Potential water and aerosol sources should be identified from movement histories.
Cases should be reported through the national surveillance arrangements.
Environmental sampling may support source investigation.
Roles and responsibilities should be coordinated across health protection and enforcement bodies.
Control measures should be adapted to the evidence and setting.
A positive urinary antigen or water-system result alone does not prove a source link.
Conclusions require case definition, movements, timing, clinical isolates, environmental samples and epidemiological linkage.
Adult social-care providers should report qualifying acute respiratory infection outbreaks.
Care homes, supported living and extra-care settings may use the reporting pathway where available.
Outbreak identification depends on linked respiratory illness in the setting.
Reports support timely health-protection and infection-control advice.
Existing outbreaks can be updated through the service or local arrangements.
Urgent clinical concerns require appropriate medical escalation.
Providers outside supported online regions should use local health-protection arrangements.
Records of onset, symptoms, testing and affected residents support assessment.
A single cough or positive test does not automatically define a setting outbreak.
Conclusions require case count, linkage, timing, setting, symptoms, testing and public-health assessment.
Food-contact materials must comply with applicable safety and authorisation requirements.
The official GB register lists substances authorised for plastic food-contact materials.
Authorisations can specify identity, restrictions and conditions of use.
Businesses should use the current official register when checking permitted substances.
Migration and intended-use conditions are relevant to safety assessment.
Traceability and supporting documentation should identify the material and supplier.
Changes in formulation or use can affect compliance.
Unauthorised substances should not be assumed safe for food-contact use.
A recycling symbol or supplier statement does not prove regulatory compliance.
Conclusions require exact substance, material, intended use, migration, authorisation, conditions and documentation evidence.
Food supplements are foods and must comply with relevant food law.
Businesses should identify all ingredients and their intended use.
Safety responsibilities apply to vitamins, minerals, botanicals and other supplement ingredients.
Labels and claims must meet the applicable legal requirements.
Novel ingredients may require authorisation before market placement.
Contaminants and excessive ingredient levels can create safety concerns.
Supplier assurance and product specifications support compliance.
Adverse information and complaints should trigger review and corrective action.
A supplement label or natural-origin claim does not establish safety.
Product conclusions require ingredients, dose, population, claims, contaminants, authorisation and manufacturing evidence.
